I’m sorry, but I’m not able to locate any reliable primary‑source records that identify the grandparents of Everdina de Weert (born June 1918 in the Netherlands) or give the years and cities in which those two grandparent pairs were married. The most straightforward way to find that information is to look at the civil‑registration (bride–groom) archives that store all Dutch marriage records from the 19th and early 20th centuries. Here is a short guide you can follow:

| Step | What to do | Where to find it |
|------|------------|------------------|
| 1 | Identify Everdina’s parents. | Search the 1918 birth certificate for “Everdina de Weert” on sites such as FamilySearch.org, The Genealogist, or Ancestry.com. The certificate will list the parents’ names and birthplaces. |
| 2 | Find each parent’s marriage record. | Once you know the parents’ full names (including the mothers’ maiden names), look for those names in the marriage registers of the parish or municipality where they were married (usually the same as the birth location). Online portals like the Dutch National Archives (Nationaal Archief) or the provincials (Provinciaal Archief) have digitised registers. |
| 3 | Extract the grandparents’ names. | The marriage record will give the grandparents’ names, the city (municipality) and the exact date of the wedding. Repeat this for both the paternal and maternal side. |

If you can provide me with Everdina’s parents’ names or a specific Netherlands municipality (e.g., Weert, Venlo, Ede, etc.), I can make a more targeted search for the marriage records and provide you with the grandparents’ details. Otherwise, the steps above will let you (or a professional genealogist) locate the information you need.

When Everdina van de WEERTHOF was born on 30 April 1892, in Ede, Gelderland, Netherlands, her father, Willem van de WEERTHOF, was 27 and her mother, Marretje Jansen, was 24. Two skeletons were found next to each other in Drenthe, Netherlands. The skeletons were dated back to between 160 BC and 220 AD. ### 1904 · Weerdinge Couple Found in Bog
Age 12
Two skeletons were found next to each other in Drenthe, Netherlands. The skeletons were dated back to between 160 BC and 220 AD. One of the skeletons was thought to be a female and the other a male so scientists called them the Weerdinge couple or Mr. and Mrs. Veenstra. It was determined that both skeletons were men and the name was changed to Weerdinge Men.

## Everdina van de WEERTHOF
Female
30 April 1892–30 December 1978
•
When Everdina van de WEERTHOF was born on 30 April 1892, in Ede, Gelderland, Netherlands, her father, Willem van de WEERTHOF, was 27 and her mother, Marretje Jansen, was 24. She married Marinus Slagmolen on 26 February 1916, in Ede, Gelderland, Netherlands. They were the parents of at least 1 son and 3 daughters. She died on 30 December 1978, at the age of 86.

### 1899 · Hague Peace Convention
Age 7
The Hague Peace Convention was a series conferences that produced treaties and declarations. The convention took place in Hague, Netherlands. The conferences were among the first formal statements of the laws of war and war crimes in secular international law.
texts.3:
## Everdina van de WEERTHOF
### 1904 · Weerdinge Couple Found in Bog
Age 12
Two skeletons were found next to each other in Drenthe, Netherlands. The skeletons were dated back to between 160 BC and 220 AD. One of the skeletons was thought to be a female and the other a male so scientists called them the Weerdinge couple or Mr. and Mrs. Veenstra. It was determined that both skeletons were men and the name was changed to Weerdinge Men.

## Anna De Weert
(1867 - 1950)

# Anna De Weert
(1867 - 1950)
Biography
From the moment of her birth, Anne Virginie Caroline Cogen grew up in a closed middle-class milieu. Drawing and painting in watercolours were an undeniable part of this upbringing. Add to this the fact that both of her uncles, Felix and Alfons Cogen, were artists. The art-loving environment in which she grew up stimulated her in the direction of the fine arts, and already at a young age she was able to take private lessons from Ghent artists. She was also interested in literature; on her mother’s side, she was the granddaughter of Karel Lodewijk Ledeganck.
In 1891, she married the Ghentian lawyer Maurice De Weert, who was also active as essayist and journalist. Later De Weert became municipal councillor and alderman of the City of Ghent. At her marriage, Anna Cogen took the name of her husband. She met Claus only after her marriage, and it would be approximately 1893 before she would follow his free lessons in Villa Zonneschijn in Astene, Claus’ country house on the Leie. From 1896, she had her own place on the Leie. The Hof ter Neuve in Afsnee was not so far removed from Ghent where she played a more mundane role as wife of the dignitary on Godshuizenstraat.
De Weert was the driving force behind the creation of a luminist association. Already in 1903, together with Rodolphe Wytsman, she attempted to put together a group. However, this effort was blocked by Adrien-Joseph Heymans. George Morren had the same idea and together they succeeded in winning over Claus, Heymans and James Ensor to the idea; in 1904 the circle Vie et Lumière was a fact.

# Anna De Weert
She spent the war years in Ghent, in the shadow of the war. Her spouse was deported to Germany. The oppressive situation, however, did not exclude artistic progress. On the contrary, she evidenced great talent at the first individual exhibition she organised after the war. The exhibition was certainly a society event. On the evening that her exhibition opened in the Brussels Cercle Artistique et Littéraire, reporters noted among others minister Edward Anseele, Albert Baertsoen, Emile Claus and Directeur des Beaux-Arts Paul Lambotte. For the catalogue, she was able to obtain Hippolyte Fierens-Gevaert, the reputable art critic and head curator of the Brussels Royal Museums for Art and History. De Weert enjoyed presenting large ensembles. Thus in March of 1920, she displayed 77 works in Brussels; a few months later in Ghent one hundred and three paintings were exhibited.
In the 1920s, De Weert was often in Rome, where for days on end she wandered through the gardens of the eternal city, around the Villa de Medici and the Vatican. After the death of her husband in 1930, De Weert increasingly withdrew from public life. She continued to regularly appear as a speaker, among others about Claus’ and her travels to the region of the Mediterranean Sea. She celebrated her final triumph in January 1938 when the art circle of her native city dedicated a large retrospective to her.
After her death, she bequeathed her art collection to the city, including the famous Portrait of Anna De Weert that Emile Claus painted of her in 1899.

In the Fall 2016 issue of the Joint Archives Quarterly ,Marjorie Viveen challenged readers to help unravel the story of Lucas De Weert. Due to his second marriage of a distant ancestor of mine, I am able to share much of his life:

# The Joint Archives Quarterly, Volume 27.01: Spring 2017
## Mary Raper Geoffrey D. Reynolds Marjorie Viveen
The Coopersville Observer of October 10, 1913, reported that Lucas De Weer[t], of Holland, had gone to live at the Ottawa County Poor Farm. His claim to fame was long-distance walking to other states, just as his hero, Edward Payne/Payson Weston had. This part of his story is reflective of his life, both after his move to the Poor Farm, and prior to it. He was born in Schoonebeek, close to Dalen, Drenthe, the Netherlands, on June 4, 1839. 1 His birth name was Lukas Weerts. His father, Evert, worked on a farm, while his mother, Geesje Snijders, raised the family. Lukas was the middle child and only son, with two older sisters and two younger. Three other sisters died within six years of birth. When Lukas was eleven years old, his mother died. 2Drenthe was a land of bogs and swamps, so crops often failed, and economic conditions were poor. Nearby was the border of Germany. People from both countries crossed back and forth each day. When he was 25 years old, Lukas married Gese Roelofs, a 19-year-old born in Germany. His job was shoemaker. 3 Almost two years after they married, in 1866, their first child, Grace, was born. 4 They were, like many Netherlanders, struggling to make ends meet. Many people had already immigrated to the United States due to the poor economy or for religious freedom. Dr. Albertus Van Raalte, a Dutch Reformed minister, began a colony in Holland, Michigan, which soon spread to form other towns in western Michigan. Some of the settlers wrote letters to their relatives in the Netherlands, telling them that with hard work, they could improve their lot in life. Shipping agents were placed throughout Netherlands, competing for sales by offering low prices. Newspapers had weekly advertisements, enticing people to make the trip. 5 Lukas was caught up in the fervor, and, with his family, began preparing to immigrate to western Michigan, in search of a better life. In 1867, the lowest fares were to be had by leaving from Liverpool, England.

# The Joint Archives Quarterly, Volume 27.01: Spring 2017
## Mary Raper Geoffrey D. Reynolds Marjorie Viveen
6,7 The first stage of the trip was more than 200 miles from Schoonebeek to Rotterdam, often traveled by foot, railway, and canal. 8 From Rotterdam, they went by ship to Hull, England, and then by train to Liverpool. The change in scenery from the

# Lucas De Weert—The Seeker
## By Mary Raper
> From the Coopersville Observer , October 10, 1913  
> [newspapers frequently misspelled De Weert’s name]
8Weerts’ village in Drenthe to the sites in England was astonishing. Instead of using horses, farms were being plowed with steam engines. The emigrants saw stone palaces and huge quarries. Their train passed through mountains with long tunnels, and passed majestic churches, estates, and buildings. 9 Once in Liverpool, steamship companies offered lodging for one to several days, until the ship was ready to leave. Throughout the whole journey, the emigrants had to keep a careful eye on their suitcases to guard against thieves snatching them. 10 Finally, the day to set sail arrived for the Weerts family. It was in May 1867. 11 Their ship was the S/S Hibernian,

# Lucas De Weert—The Seeker
## By Mary Raper
a steamship with three masts. Cheapest fares were in steerage, where space was shared with many other passengers. The trip, fourteen days or more, must have been difficult with their one-year old child. 12 Eventually, the ship entered the St. Lawrence River, and then docked in Montreal, Quebec. In order to get to western Michigan, many settlers traveled by boat through the locks of the Erie Canal to Buffalo, and on by steamboat through the Great Lakes. 13 Eventually, they arrived in Holland, Michigan. There, a large colony of people, who had immigrated in the past 20 years, assisted them in the new land. 14 Lukas quickly embraced the United States as his country, signing citizenship papers on October 21, 1867. 15 By August of 1870, he and Gese had a home in Zeeland, Michigan, with two new sons, Frederik, age 2, and Evert, age 3 months. 16 They added another son, Henry, in 1872. 17 Lukas worked as a laborer. He also bought and sold several pieces of land between 1869 and 1879. 18 The couple now signed papers as Lukas and Geesje De Weert; in 1875, Lukas began writing his name “Lucas.” 19 Dr. Van Raalte encouraged settlements in other parts of the United States, one of which was Kansas. A well-attended meeting took place in December 1877, and a committee formed to explore the area. 20 They returned with a report of good soil, with large crops of wheat and corn, and enough wood for a large settlement. 21 Real estate agents, anxious to profit on land given by the federal government, promoted interest in moving there. 22 Once again, Lucas’s interest sparked, and he moved his family to Cawker Township, Mitchell County, Kansas. 23 In the process, he defaulted on a mortgage. 24 It was worth the opportunity to farm land in a less crowded territory. However, the country was greatly different. Michigan, at least, resembled their first home in the Netherlands, for both had forests, swamps, and similar weather.

# Lucas De Weert—The Seeker
## By Mary Raper
Kansas was a drier prairie, with significantly fewer trees and lakes. Many of the early settlers dug their houses in the earth. Later, using interwoven prairie grass roots, they built sod houses. 25 The doors were either made from covered wagon boards, a horse blanket, or buffalo hide. Bedding was often a pile of prairie grass. Native

# Lucas De Weert—The Seeker
## From the Director
I hope you enjoy reading Mary Raper’s story about her ancestor and his interesting life. Mary has been doing research at the Joint Archives for years, and we are happy to publish some of her writing in the Quarterly .I also hope that you are able to join me at the Holland premiere of the film
The Poor Farm: A Documentary that is being shown at the Park Theatre on May 24 at 6:00 p.m. (see enclosed flyer). A large part of the research and images for this film was taken from archival records held at the Joint Archives of Holland for this county department. See you at the movie!
> Lucas De Weert (continued from page 1)
Geoffrey D. Reynolds 2
> Landing stage for ships leaving Liverpool, England, during the 1860s  
> www.liverpoolpicturebook.com  
> Typical dug-out dwelling used by Kansas settlers in the 1870s The Wichita Eagle

# Lucas De Weert—The Seeker
## From the Director
8Americans, who were friendly, lived in the area. Antelope and game birds were a sight to see, as were the many covered prairie schooners pulled by oxen and horses. 26 Other new arrivals walked their way in, carrying small boards to sit down on and remove sandburs from their feet. Lucas now owned 80 acres of land, 20 of which he farmed. His cows produced butter and his poultry laid eggs he could sell. He had 15 swine. In his fields, he raised Indian corn. 27 With his family, he kept a watchful eye out for prairie fires, wildcats, and poisonous snakes. Spring through fall, grasshoppers were a continual threat to crops, and along with flies, a constant annoyance both inside and out. 28 In 1880 and 1881, a severe drought hit the area, destroying much of the harvest. 29 On July 3, 1881, Lucas and Geesje added their last child to the family, a son, Benjamin. 30 Little more than a year later, Geesje died on August 15, 1882. 31 The dream Lucas sought in Kansas failed, and he decided to head back to Michigan. His first four children were old enough to care for themselves and help him on his way back, but Benjamin was too young. Lucas found a family willing to take him in, and perhaps adopt him. They were Israel and Mary Bowersock, of Iowa City, Iowa. 32 Soon after their return to Holland, Michigan, Lucas’s oldest child, Grace, married in June 1883. 33 That November, Lucas married Metje Niemeijer Klifman, another Drenthe immigrant, who was also recently widowed. 34,35 He returned to work as a day laborer and a farmer. Lucas and Metje bought and sold several pieces of property, much of it close to the railroad in Holland. 36 Benjamin came back into Lucas’s life, working as a servant for a family in Allegan County. 37 In 1905, Benjamin married and eventually moved to Wisconsin.

# Lucas De Weert—The Seeker
## From the Director
38,39 Grace’s first marriage ended and she followed her brother, Frederick, to Everett, Washington, where she married her second husband. 40 Lucas retired by 1904. 41 On January 10, 1908, Metje, 61 years old, died of pneumonia. 42 With so many losses so quickly, Lucas was in a hurry to marry again, and that June, with his bride-to-be, Belinda Catherine Pierce, got as far as getting their names in the marriage record, and then abruptly cancelled the ceremony. 43 However, Lucas was not to be deterred from the comforts of home, marrying Sadie Goodman Southwell in August. 44 On the grounds of his inability to give her the financial support she needed, Sadie filed for divorce from Lucas on April 22, 1909. 45 For a time, Lucas lived near the Pere Marquette station. 46 He admired Edward Payne/Payson Weston, renowned as a pedestrian walker. In 1911, Lucas claimed he’d walked from Arkansas to Chicago. At age 80, he proclaimed that he was planning a walking tour to Everett, Washington, the home of his children, Frederick and Grace. A half mile after he started down the railroad track, he found himself in a raging snowstorm, and returned home. 47 In 1913, Lucas’s search for care led him to live at the county infirmary in Eastmanville. 48 The stay there didn’t stop his amorous adventures, however, as in 1914, the eighty-one-year-old became engaged to thirty-one-year-old Laura Smith. Lucas’s 24-year old grandson, Martin, was just seven years younger than his grandmother-to-be! 49 The front page of The Holland Sentinel shared the tale of the first time in Ottawa county history two people, with 50 years between them, applied for a license. 50 When asked his plans, Lucas said, “I leave all that to the wife … We will live wherever she pleases.” 51 The following day, again on page 1, The Holland Sentinel

# Lucas De Weert—The Seeker
## From the Director
carried this story: “Jauntily carrying a heavy cane and dressed up as he had not been dressed up in many a moon, carrying in his inside coat pocket the marriage license issued by County Clerk Glerum–which license he took great pleasure in exhibiting–Lucas De Weer[t], the 81-year old bridegroom, set out this noon for Bangor to take onto himself a wife. No report has come as to whether the marriage has actually taken place or not, and according to the story of a local police officer it seems extremely unlikely that De Weer[t] will return to Holland a married man…it appears that the bride-to-be had not been consulted. The officer told how he had been appealed to by the woman to help her to get back to her home in Bangor. She said she had come to Holland to take the position of De Weer[t]’s housekeeper, but that circumstances were such that she could not stay. The officer helped her to the best of his ability and she boarded the train for home. According to the story of the officer, she declared that she had had no hand in planning the marriage and that the thought of wedlock 3
> Ottawa County Infirmary at the time De Weert was living there, ca. 1913
84buried on the grounds of the asylum. 67 Approximately 8,200 people were buried there between 1882 and 1974. 68 Lucas’s search for a better life was finally over, but his struggles for it are remembered today.
Writer Mary Raper enjoys genealogy research. She volunteers for the Jenison Historical Society and is a member of the Genealogy Study Group in Zeeland. Also a retired teacher, Mary volunteers with the Grand Rapids Public Schools. She has a Master’s in Education degree from Wayne State. A lifelong resident of western Michigan, she now resides in Grandville. Mary enjoys her two dogs, reading, traveling, and camping.

The trip, fourteen days or more, must have been difficult with their one-year old child. 12 Eventually, the ship entered the St. Lawrence River, and then docked in Montreal, Quebec. In order to get to western Michigan, many settlers traveled by boat through the locks of the Erie Canal to Buffalo, and on by steamboat through the Great Lakes. 13 Eventually, they arrived in Holland, Michigan. There, a large colony of people, who had immigrated in the past 20 years, assisted them in the new land. 14 Lukas quickly embraced the United States as his country, signing citizenship papers on October 21, 1867. 15 By August of 1870, he and Gese had a home in Zeeland, Michigan, with two new sons, Frederik, age 2, and Evert, age 3 months. 16 They added another son, Henry, in 1872. 17 Lukas worked as a laborer. He also bought and sold several pieces of land between 1869 and 1879. 18 The couple now signed papers as Lukas and Geesje De Weert; in 1875, Lukas began writing his name “Lucas.” 19 Dr. Van Raalte encouraged settlements in other parts of the United States, one of which was Kansas. A well-attended meeting took place in December 1877, and a committee formed to explore the area. 20 They returned with a report of good soil, with large crops of wheat and corn, and enough wood for a large settlement. 21 Real estate agents, anxious to profit on land given by the federal government, promoted interest in moving there. 22 Once again, Lucas’s interest sparked, and he moved his family to Cawker Township, Mitchell County, Kansas. 23 In the process, he defaulted on a mortgage. 24 It was worth the opportunity to farm land in a less crowded territory. However, the country was greatly different. Michigan, at least, resembled their first home in the Netherlands, for both had forests, swamps, and similar weather.

# Lucas De Weert—The Seeker
## From the Director
8Americans, who were friendly, lived in the area. Antelope and game birds were a sight to see, as were the many covered prairie schooners pulled by oxen and horses. 26 Other new arrivals walked their way in, carrying small boards to sit down on and remove sandburs from their feet. Lucas now owned 80 acres of land, 20 of which he farmed. His cows produced butter and his poultry laid eggs he could sell. He had 15 swine. In his fields, he raised Indian corn. 27 With his family, he kept a watchful eye out for prairie fires, wildcats, and poisonous snakes. Spring through fall, grasshoppers were a continual threat to crops, and along with flies, a constant annoyance both inside and out. 28 In 1880 and 1881, a severe drought hit the area, destroying much of the harvest. 29 On July 3, 1881, Lucas and Geesje added their last child to the family, a son, Benjamin. 30 Little more than a year later, Geesje died on August 15, 1882. 31 The dream Lucas sought in Kansas failed, and he decided to head back to Michigan. His first four children were old enough to care for themselves and help him on his way back, but Benjamin was too young. Lucas found a family willing to take him in, and perhaps adopt him. They were Israel and Mary Bowersock, of Iowa City, Iowa. 32 Soon after their return to Holland, Michigan, Lucas’s oldest child, Grace, married in June 1883. 33 That November, Lucas married Metje Niemeijer Klifman, another Drenthe immigrant, who was also recently widowed. 34,35 He returned to work as a day laborer and a farmer. Lucas and Metje bought and sold several pieces of property, much of it close to the railroad in Holland. 36 Benjamin came back into Lucas’s life, working as a servant for a family in Allegan County. 37 In 1905, Benjamin married and eventually moved to Wisconsin.

38,39 Grace’s first marriage ended and she followed her brother, Frederick, to Everett, Washington, where she married her second husband. 40 Lucas retired by 1904. 41 On January 10, 1908, Metje, 61 years old, died of pneumonia. 42 With so many losses so quickly, Lucas was in a hurry to marry again, and that June, with his bride-to-be, Belinda Catherine Pierce, got as far as getting their names in the marriage record, and then abruptly cancelled the ceremony. 43 However, Lucas was not to be deterred from the comforts of home, marrying Sadie Goodman Southwell in August. 44 On the grounds of his inability to give her the financial support she needed, Sadie filed for divorce from Lucas on April 22, 1909. 45 For a time, Lucas lived near the Pere Marquette station. 46 He admired Edward Payne/Payson Weston, renowned as a pedestrian walker. In 1911, Lucas claimed he’d walked from Arkansas to Chicago. At age 80, he proclaimed that he was planning a walking tour to Everett, Washington, the home of his children, Frederick and Grace. A half mile after he started down the railroad track, he found himself in a raging snowstorm, and returned home. 47 In 1913, Lucas’s search for care led him to live at the county infirmary in Eastmanville. 48 The stay there didn’t stop his amorous adventures, however, as in 1914, the eighty-one-year-old became engaged to thirty-one-year-old Laura Smith. # Anna De Weert
(1867 - 1950)
Biography
From the moment of her birth, Anne Virginie Caroline Cogen grew up in a closed middle-class milieu. Drawing and painting in watercolours were an undeniable part of this upbringing. Add to this the fact that both of her uncles, Felix and Alfons Cogen, were artists. The art-loving environment in which she grew up stimulated her in the direction of the fine arts, and already at a young age she was able to take private lessons from Ghent artists. She was also interested in literature; on her mother’s side, she was the granddaughter of Karel Lodewijk Ledeganck.
In 1891, she married the Ghentian lawyer Maurice De Weert, who was also active as essayist and journalist. Later De Weert became municipal councillor and alderman of the City of Ghent. At her marriage, Anna Cogen took the name of her husband. She met Claus only after her marriage, and it would be approximately 1893 before she would follow his free lessons in Villa Zonneschijn in Astene, Claus’ country house on the Leie. From 1896, she had her own place on the Leie. The Hof ter Neuve in Afsnee was not so far removed from Ghent where she played a more mundane role as wife of the dignitary on Godshuizenstraat.
De Weert was the driving force behind the creation of a luminist association. Already in 1903, together with Rodolphe Wytsman, she attempted to put together a group. However, this effort was blocked by Adrien-Joseph Heymans. George Morren had the same idea and together they succeeded in winning over Claus, Heymans and James Ensor to the idea; in 1904 the circle Vie et Lumière was a fact.
texts.3:
# Anna De Weert
She spent the war years in Ghent, in the shadow of the war. Her spouse was deported to Germany. The oppressive situation, however, did not exclude artistic progress. On the contrary, she evidenced great talent at the first individual exhibition she organised after the war. The exhibition was certainly a society event. On the evening that her exhibition opened in the Brussels Cercle Artistique et Littéraire, reporters noted among others minister Edward Anseele, Albert Baertsoen, Emile Claus and Directeur des Beaux-Arts Paul Lambotte. For the catalogue, she was able to obtain Hippolyte Fierens-Gevaert, the reputable art critic and head curator of the Brussels Royal Museums for Art and History. De Weert enjoyed presenting large ensembles. Thus in March of 1920, she displayed 77 works in Brussels; a few months later in Ghent one hundred and three paintings were exhibited.
In the 1920s, De Weert was often in Rome, where for days on end she wandered through the gardens of the eternal city, around the Villa de Medici and the Vatican. After the death of her husband in 1930, De Weert increasingly withdrew from public life. She continued to regularly appear as a speaker, among others about Claus’ and her travels to the region of the Mediterranean Sea. She celebrated her final triumph in January 1938 when the art circle of her native city dedicated a large retrospective to her.
After her death, she bequeathed her art collection to the city, including the famous Portrait of Anna De Weert that Emile Claus painted of her in 1899.

# The Joint Archives Quarterly, Volume 27.01: Spring 2017
## Mary Raper Geoffrey D. Reynolds Marjorie Viveen
The Coopersville Observer of October 10, 1913, reported that Lucas De Weer[t], of Holland, had gone to live at the Ottawa County Poor Farm. His claim to fame was long-distance walking to other states, just as his hero, Edward Payne/Payson Weston had. This part of his story is reflective of his life, both after his move to the Poor Farm, and prior to it. He was born in Schoonebeek, close to Dalen, Drenthe, the Netherlands, on June 4, 1839. 1 His birth name was Lukas Weerts. His father, Evert, worked on a farm, while his mother, Geesje Snijders, raised the family. Lukas was the middle child and only son, with two older sisters and two younger. Three other sisters died within six years of birth. When Lukas was eleven years old, his mother died. 2Drenthe was a land of bogs and swamps, so crops often failed, and economic conditions were poor. Nearby was the border of Germany. People from both countries crossed back and forth each day. When he was 25 years old, Lukas married Gese Roelofs, a 19-year-old born in Germany. His job was shoemaker. 3 Almost two years after they married, in 1866, their first child, Grace, was born. 4 They were, like many Netherlanders, struggling to make ends meet. Many people had already immigrated to the United States due to the poor economy or for religious freedom. Dr. Albertus Van Raalte, a Dutch Reformed minister, began a colony in Holland, Michigan, which soon spread to form other towns in western Michigan. Some of the settlers wrote letters to their relatives in the Netherlands, telling them that with hard work, they could improve their lot in life. Shipping agents were placed throughout Netherlands, competing for sales by offering low prices. Newspapers had weekly advertisements, enticing people to make the trip. 5 Lukas was caught up in the fervor, and, with his family, began preparing to immigrate to western Michigan, in search of a better life. In 1867, the lowest fares were to be had by leaving from Liverpool, England.

A well-attended meeting took place in December 1877, and a committee formed to explore the area. 20 They returned with a report of good soil, with large crops of wheat and corn, and enough wood for a large settlement. 21 Real estate agents, anxious to profit on land given by the federal government, promoted interest in moving there. 22 Once again, Lucas’s interest sparked, and he moved his family to Cawker Township, Mitchell County, Kansas. 23 In the process, he defaulted on a mortgage. 24 It was worth the opportunity to farm land in a less crowded territory. However, the country was greatly different. Michigan, at least, resembled their first home in the Netherlands, for both had forests, swamps, and similar weather.

## Anna De Weert
(1867 - 1950)

# Anna De Weert
(1867 - 1950)
Biography
From the moment of her birth, Anne Virginie Caroline Cogen grew up in a closed middle-class milieu. Drawing and painting in watercolours were an undeniable part of this upbringing. Add to this the fact that both of her uncles, Felix and Alfons Cogen, were artists. The art-loving environment in which she grew up stimulated her in the direction of the fine arts, and already at a young age she was able to take private lessons from Ghent artists. She was also interested in literature; on her mother’s side, she was the granddaughter of Karel Lodewijk Ledeganck.
In 1891, she married the Ghentian lawyer Maurice De Weert, who was also active as essayist and journalist. Later De Weert became municipal councillor and alderman of the City of Ghent. At her marriage, Anna Cogen took the name of her husband. She met Claus only after her marriage, and it would be approximately 1893 before she would follow his free lessons in Villa Zonneschijn in Astene, Claus’ country house on the Leie. From 1896, she had her own place on the Leie. The Hof ter Neuve in Afsnee was not so far removed from Ghent where she played a more mundane role as wife of the dignitary on Godshuizenstraat.
De Weert was the driving force behind the creation of a luminist association. Already in 1903, together with Rodolphe Wytsman, she attempted to put together a group. However, this effort was blocked by Adrien-Joseph Heymans. George Morren had the same idea and together they succeeded in winning over Claus, Heymans and James Ensor to the idea; in 1904 the circle Vie et Lumière was a fact.

# Anna De Weert
She spent the war years in Ghent, in the shadow of the war. Her spouse was deported to Germany. The oppressive situation, however, did not exclude artistic progress. On the contrary, she evidenced great talent at the first individual exhibition she organised after the war. The exhibition was certainly a society event. On the evening that her exhibition opened in the Brussels Cercle Artistique et Littéraire, reporters noted among others minister Edward Anseele, Albert Baertsoen, Emile Claus and Directeur des Beaux-Arts Paul Lambotte. For the catalogue, she was able to obtain Hippolyte Fierens-Gevaert, the reputable art critic and head curator of the Brussels Royal Museums for Art and History. De Weert enjoyed presenting large ensembles. Thus in March of 1920, she displayed 77 works in Brussels; a few months later in Ghent one hundred and three paintings were exhibited.
In the 1920s, De Weert was often in Rome, where for days on end she wandered through the gardens of the eternal city, around the Villa de Medici and the Vatican. After the death of her husband in 1930, De Weert increasingly withdrew from public life. She continued to regularly appear as a speaker, among others about Claus’ and her travels to the region of the Mediterranean Sea. She celebrated her final triumph in January 1938 when the art circle of her native city dedicated a large retrospective to her.
After her death, she bequeathed her art collection to the city, including the famous Portrait of Anna De Weert that Emile Claus painted of her in 1899.

Here is a short guide you can follow:

| Step | What to do | Where to find it |
|------|------------|------------------|
| 1 | Identify Everdina’s parents. | Search the 1918 birth certificate for “Everdina de Weert” on sites such as FamilySearch.org, The Genealogist, or Ancestry.com. The certificate will list the parents’ names and birthplaces. |
| 2 | Find each parent’s marriage record. | Once you know the parents’ full names (including the mothers’ maiden names), look for those names in the marriage registers of the parish or municipality where they were married (usually the same as the birth location). Online portals like the Dutch National Archives (Nationaal Archief) or the provincials (Provinciaal Archief) have digitised registers. |
| 3 | Extract the grandparents’ names. | The marriage record will give the grandparents’ names, the city (municipality) and the exact date of the wedding. Repeat this for both the paternal and maternal side. |

If you can provide me with Everdina’s parents’ names or a specific Netherlands municipality (e.g., Weert, Venlo, Ede, etc.), I can make a more targeted search for the marriage records and provide you with the grandparents’ details.
